title: How many projects have you cancelled thanks to AI?
author: klas-klattermus
selftext:
Within two months I've managed to cancel at least ten projects, which probably would have taken me a month or two each to give up on if I didn't have AI!

A normal person might feel discouraged but I think it's great, I can prototype rapidly and learn from mistakes without wasting years of my life!

comments.author: n3cr0n_k1tt3n
comments.body: Rather than learning and finishing a project you decided to give up on all of them?

replies.author: klas-klattermus
replies.body: Only the ones that weren't fun enough. I like experimental ideas, for an example I was working on a story driven underwater survival horror game where the player surface is cards (think cultist simulator or witch hand) but after trying it out I realized that while I could make it atmospheric, that was thanks to the event/storytelling system and that the way I structured it as a card game and also survival in the form of management didn't really vibe with the horror theme. So instead of pushing forward I decided to decouple the card slice so I can reuse it for another project if needed and also keep the event graph system. The theme works and the event system works, but I will probably try a wizardry interaction surface instead and scale down the survival/crafting elements.

replies.author: Fun_Worry_3079
replies.body:
One thing you have to watch for when designing a game is whether or not your mechanics and theme can fill the same space. 

For example, on “Birdie Blues & the Jazz Cats,” I made sure that, when I developed a mechanic, it could seamlessly integrate into the next mechanic (catching music notes came first, inspired by “Popeye;” throwing them at enemies, inspired by “Bubble Bobble,” came next when I needed something to do with the music notes, other than gain points).

My advice to you is do some research into the genre of game you want to make and ask yourself, “can I make these mechanics flow and make logical sense?” If you can (without having to reach), then build it. Otherwise, go back to the drawing board until you can find a mechanic that fits.

Long story short, have a thematic element in place before you “touch” a line of code. You’ll be less likely to scrap projects that way!

replies.author: klas-klattermus
replies.body: It's sound advice, thank you

replies.author: klas-klattermus
replies.body: Oh I've done that plenty, it's not that I give up because it's too hard but rather that the experimental game concepts didn't work out in the end for some of my projects. Also three of those projects were also different takes on management tools where I tried different approaches such as canvas boards with modular plugins with different tech stacks (electron vite and winui3) and in the end I took my experiences and ended up making it into a webapp instead with a simpler interaction surface and better suited for concurrent editing.

replies.author: klas-klattermus

comments.author: Aesthetic-Engine
comments.body:
I cancelled one project because I realized I was missing some key design elements and I had a better idea I wanted to pursue. 

The only other project I cancelled was because I found out one of the tools my agent helped choose for the project was actually going to be legally murky to include in the stack instead of having a clean MIT license. 

Each time though I learned a ton and I did a full retrospective by exporting my chat logs and having Opus 4.6 review them and produce an incredibly valuable report that pointed out mistakes and opportunities for improvement.

replies.author: klas-klattermus
replies.body: Nice, yeah and just the meta-knowledge of the mistakes we do when using the AI themselves is valuable knowledge!

comments.author: Fun_Worry_3079
comments.body: I’ve never fully canceled a project, but I have scrapped full concepts/codebases before and started from scratch. In fact, that’s happened on my last three projects: “Spree,” “Birdie Blues,” and my latest game (codename “Yardwork”). I took what I learned from the original iteration, however, in order to make the next version even better.

replies.author: klas-klattermus
replies.body: Totally valid, and it's so nice that we can just try out a tech stack and easily switch to something else. Did you switch engine or decide to code your own or how come you scrapped them?

replies.author: Fun_Worry_3079
replies.body: No, nothing like that. I scrapped them because the concepts and high-level ideas I had for those projects simply wasn’t panning out as I hoped, or I would simply discover an easier and more streamlined method to development. As far as taking what I learned goes, there are tricks and methods I’ve learned on previous projects that still find their way into my current ones!

comments.author: nhami
comments.body:

Once I finish working in the projects I am working now. I plan to return to my unfinished projects to work on them with my knowledge and skill.

replies.author: klas-klattermus

comments.author: iiithewizardiii
comments.body:
I agree it's a good thing. I've started and cancelled way more than usual, because I'm able to get to playable way faster, then make a solid determination of the moment we all ask "is this anything?"

That said, it ALSO led to me working on more than one greenlit game at the same time, which is new.

replies.author: klas-klattermus
replies.body: Exactly, not every idea is valid but it also feels so good to just try out even the crazy ideas to see if there's anything worth salvaging. I tried out a new mechanic and it kind of works but I put it in a game where it doesn't shine, but all I lost was a few days of promoting in between work. Yeah the multiple project part is crazy nice, good job on actually getting greenlit, best of luck to you!

comments.author: StunningGold8030
comments.body: Lot of negative comments when tinkering games should be fun. Anyway I get what you mean. I've been an indiedev for several decades and I have cancelled so many games. Please that hate AI will say it's useless but it just accelerates your development, if the project will fail it will fail faster. Last year I started integrating it here and there, about 6 months ago I fully moved my dev workflow into AI. I haven't felt less stressed and happier about developing before. Prompts are my language now, and putting the load of having the whole game logic in my mind is no longer an issue. It might have taken me about a year to cancel a project, now it's taking 2 months. Yeah, it's great to prototype and release samples for the market to judge whether they want my games or not. I'm becoming increasingly more ambitious which I previously restrained of.

replies.author: klas-klattermus
replies.body: Heck yes, saves you time to find that one concept that works

replies.author: StunningGold8030
replies.body: That's the basis of quality, to try, test and reject.
